You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Liberty

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'liberty' primarily symbolizes the spiritual freedom believers receive in Christ: emancipation from bondage to sin, death, condemnation, and the law as a means of justification. It is freedom for holiness and love, not autonomy or license — the redeemed state of the children of God enabled by the Spirit.",

    "Galatians 5:1 ('For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery')",

    "John 8:31-36 ('If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed')",
    "2 Corinthians 3:17 ('Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty')",
    "Romans 8:2 ('The law of the Spirit of life has set you free from the law of sin and death')",
    "Romans 8:21 ('the glorious liberty of the children of God')",
    "Romans 6:18-22 (set free from sin, become slaves of righteousness)",
    "Luke 4:18 (Jesus proclaims 'liberty to the captives,' citing Isaiah 61:1)",
    "James 1:25; 2:12 ('the perfect law of liberty')",
    "1 Peter 2:16 ('Live as free people, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil')"
  ],
  "alternatives": [

        "Isaiah 61:1-2",
        "Luke 4:18-21 (Jesus applying the Jubilee proclamation to himself)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Christian liberty of conscience — freedom in matters indifferent (adiaphora), i.e., freedom from human religious regulations regarding food, days, and ceremonies, exercised with restraint for the sake of weaker believers. Strongly developed in Reformation theology (e.g., Luther's 'Freedom of a Christian', Westminster Confession ch. 20).",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 14:1-23",
        "1 Corinthians 8:1-13; 10:23-33",
        "Colossians 2:16-23",
        "Galatians 2:4-5"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Socio-political and economic liberation — liberation theology reads biblical liberty as God's action to free the poor and oppressed from unjust structures, taking the Exodus and the Jubilee/Nazareth manifesto as paradigms.",
      "basis": [
        "Exodus 3:7-8; 6:6-7 (deliverance from Egyptian bondage)",
        "Luke 4:18-19",
        "Leviticus 25",
        "Isaiah 58:6"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Civil or national political liberty — reading biblical liberty texts as endorsing constitutional or national freedom (e.g., Leviticus 25:10 on the Liberty Bell; patriotic use of 2 Corinthians 3:17 and Galatians 5:1). Common in popular civil-religious usage but generally rejected by exegetes as the texts' meaning.",
      "basis": [
        "Leviticus 25:10 (as popularly appropriated)",
        "2 Corinthians 3:17 (as popularly appropriated)",
        "Galatians 5:1 (as popularly appropriated)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Liberty as license (libertinism) — a distorted reading, explicitly condemned in the New Testament, that treats freedom in Christ as permission to sin; recognized in interpretation history mainly as the error the epistles warn against.",
      "basis": [
        "Galatians 5:13",
        "1 Peter 2:16",
        "2 Peter 2:19 ('promising them freedom, while they themselves are slaves of corruption')",
        "Jude 4",
        "Romans 6:1-2"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad, cross-traditional agreement (patristic, Catholic, Orthodox, Reformation, and evangelical) that biblical 'liberty' means spiritual freedom from sin, death, and the law's condemnation through Christ, exercised in love and service. The main interpretive divergences concern emphasis rather than the core meaning: Reformation traditions foreground liberty of conscience; liberation theology foregrounds socio-economic liberation; popular civil religion appropriates the term for political freedom, a use most exegetes treat as anachronistic. The Greek term behind most NT uses is eleutheria; 'liberty' and 'freedom' are translation variants of the same concept (KJV favors 'liberty')."
}

  "notes": "There is a broad consensus that biblical liberty primarily signifies freedom in and through Christ, especially freedom from sin and spiritual bondage. It is not a single fixed symbol with one exclusive referent: different passages emphasize freedom from sin, the law’s condemnation, oppressive conditions, corruption, or constraints on conscience. Christian teaching generally distinguishes liberty from autonomous self-indulgence and presents it as freedom for holiness, love, and service."

BOOK ENTRY
The King's jubilee release from bondage to sin into God's household, inheritance, and faithful service. It changes masters rather than abolishing all authority; liberty is neither a license to sin nor freedom from the law's obligations.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Lev 25:10; Isa 61:1; Jas 1:25; 2 Pet 2:19) · see Liberty, ch. 19

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Leviticus 25:10 — And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family.
Isaiah 61:1 — The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
James 1:25 — But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.
2 Peter 2:19 — While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption: for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
